falas.txt: Lock one. The layers.
A chip can't be plugged straight into a computer.

tit: Under every chip: *a tiny skyscraper* of wiring.

falas.txt: The connections on the chip are far too small. The connections on the board are far too big.
So between them sits a part called the substrate. Its job is to fan thousands of tiny connections out into bigger ones.
Zoom in, and it's built like a skyscraper. A layer of copper wiring. Then a layer of insulation. Then copper again.
Over and over, with tiny holes drilled by laser to connect one floor to the next.
That insulation is the film. Every floor of the skyscraper stands on it.

v.k: Every floor stands on *the film*.

falas.txt: If the insulation is uneven, the wiring on top of it is uneven.
And one bad floor ruins the whole building.

v.l2: one bad floor ruins the building.

falas.txt: So the film has to be perfectly flat, perfectly clean, and exactly the same, every single time.

v.k: Flat. Clean. *Exactly the same*, every time.

falas.txt: Lock two. The recipe.
In the nineteen nineties, that insulation wasn't a film. It was a liquid. An ink.
You spread it on, and waited for it to dry.
It was slow. It picked up dust. And it didn't dry perfectly flat.
The chip industry wanted something better. A solid film you could just press on.
In nineteen ninety six, a chipmaker asked a very unlikely company to make one.

v.k: 1996: a chipmaker asks *a very unlikely company*.

falas.txt: Ajinomoto had been making M-S-G since nineteen oh nine.
Making it leaves behind a lot of chemistry. And since the nineteen seventies, the company had been studying what else that chemistry could do.
Some of it turned out to make excellent resins. The kind used in electronics.

v.k: Seasoning chemistry made *excellent resins*.

falas.txt: So when the request came, a young researcher named Shigeo Nakamura took it on.
He picked a resin so unstable, it had to be kept in a deep freezer. He later called that choice young and naive.

v.k: A resin that had to live *in a deep freezer*.

falas.txt: It worked. According to Ajinomoto, the film was perfected in four months.

v.k: Perfected in *four months*.

falas.txt: It went on sale in nineteen ninety nine.
So the recipe isn't one invention you can look up.
It sits on top of ninety years of chemistry, that started with soup.

v.sub: Ninety years of chemistry that started with soup.

falas.txt: Lock three. The standard.
In nineteen ninety nine, the biggest processor maker in the world adopted the film.

v.rot: ADOPTED BY THE LARGEST CPU MAKER

falas.txt: Nakamura assumed it would stay in production for about ten years.

v.cab: HOW LONG THE FILM HAS LASTED

falas.txt: That was twenty seven years ago.
Here's why it never left.
The companies that build substrates set up their whole factories around this one film. Their presses. Their lasers. Their chemical baths.
The chip designers then design their chips for those substrates.
And every new chip is tested for months on that exact combination, before a single one ships.
Change the film, and you don't change one part. You restart all of that.

v.k: Change the film, and you *restart all of that*.
